utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you are to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, I hope your health is somewhat better today. Let us try and complete this task of ours as soon as possible. I will try to deal only with military matters, since you were a brigade commander, and that is all. Shortly, I want to go back to the 65 ter document 023026, which is P332, shown to you by my learned friend, Mr. Waespi, during the examination-in-chief. This is a document from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 15th of April, 1995. It is a regular combat report for that date. Mr. Waespi told you that on that day a member of the French Battalion was killed. Do you remember that? I believe you confirmed that for us.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at item 2, "Our forces." Activities of the 12th and the 14th Division are discussed, and they were a part of the 1st Corps. It is said that at a certain hour they began with offensive activities or offensive combat activities. You, I presume, are familiar with the fact that there were combat activities on that day, on the part of the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if it could be scrolled up so the date of the document is visible for the witness, which is important for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is on the top, 15th of April; it is not at the bottom. It is in the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you confirmed another thing to Mr. Waespi, or rather, the thing I have already stated, the killing of a French soldier. It is in item 2 -- so item 1, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 2, it says, "By sniping from Grbavica, a French soldier from the UN was killed." At that time Grbavica was controlled by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm telling you. It's a document of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Further below, in item 3, it says that in the area of responsibility of the 12th and the 14th Division of your corps, at 1930 hours, they began with active combat operations. Do you know whether there were any serious clashes that day between the two opposing sides?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 1, third paragraph, it says, "In the area of responsibility of the 14th division, Serbian forces began intensive operations at 7.00, using their artillery to attack the facilities at Treskavica hill."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that. That is not what I was trying to ask you.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our forces carried out a counter-attack because of what was taking place at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I think the counsel referred to item 2, "Our forces," that's where he was quoting from, the attack at 1930 in the evening; that can be found in the second paragraph of the second heading, "Nase Snage," "Our forces," and I think the witness refers to another paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that reflected on the screen, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not yet. If we scroll down in the B/C/S version, we might come to the second paragraph. Yes. That's where you see at the bottom, "1930," and I think that is what counsel wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could we have the English synchronised with the B/C/S? It's not possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sure it's possible. I think in the English we have to go up. And, in fact, we have to go to the previous page in the English, which is the first page. Now -- sorry, it was correct, just before we switched. It's at the top of the second page, if we can go back. Yes. "In the area of responsibility, 14th Division," and then it talks about an action at 1930. I understood that's what counsel was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Waespi. I see it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you said yourself now that in the morning, at 7.00 in the morning, when the operations began, you initiated your defensive operations simultaneously. Is that correct? You just said that without being prompted by any question of mine.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that in the third paragraph of item 1, under "Aggressor," it says, "The Serbian forces launched a morning attack on our forces." It is logical if they attacked us that we had to respond. We couldn't keep silent. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this: In Sarajevo itself, were the brigades linked up in terms of communications, by wire, so as to be able to coordinate when a certain operation would be initiated?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigades were not linked between -- or rather, with each other, but we were all linked up with the -- or to the system of our command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In my hands, Mr. Hadzic, I am holding an order by Rizvo Pleh, who was the Chief of Staff, dated the 25th [as interpreted] of May, 1995. It is, therefore, an order of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is DD00-0909. We are awaiting a translation, and we have been promised to receive it on the 9th of March. It is a very short document, and I wanted to put it to you. That is the document, dated the 20th of May, 1995. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "Bearing in mind the importance of communication links in command and control and the units under combat condition, I hereby order that all vital facilitates, Grdonj, Borje, Colina Kapa, Debelo Brdo, Mojmilo, Azici, Stupsko Brdo, Vis, Zuc, the faculty of road transport, have to have wire connection to two sides -- or from two sides." Is what I have just read out correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, Rizvo Pleh ordered that these locations had to have communication links with their respective commands as well as with the command of the 12th Division via brigade commands, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, for your cross-examination, you have, at the most, another 28, 29 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will do my best. However, if I use a couple of more minutes than that, I hope you will bear with me. I kindly ask you to bear with me because this is one of the very few officers who were at that level. We may have only one other brigade commander on the entire witness list. I believe it is very important for us to hear those witnesses and -- but, however, I will try to meet your deadline. In item 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see you cross-examining him on matters that directly relate to the charges. I mean, merely establishing that orders were issued for attacks will not, in my view at any rate, advance your case. There must be attacks which relate to the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anything done by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- anything and everything done by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina [as interpreted] warranted only a military response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean by that? The response from the -- the response from the Serb army must be a response related to one of the incidents, and then you would be seeking to say that that response was a defensive response; then it will become relevant and could lead to your client walking through the doors a free man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I was trying to do. My colleague is telling me there is a part of the transcript missing. Instead of the "army of Bosnia and Herzegovina," it should read the "army of the Bosnian Serbs." All they tried to do was to defend themselves, and it was never their goal to open fire on Sarajevo without any reason. That is the entire case of ours, and I'm trying to put it forth by way of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, proceed. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can correct the transcript then, page 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript will have recorded the correction. I don't know the -- the transcript would have recorded the correction that you made. I'm not aware that there is any technical possibility to correct it now, but in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document, DD00-0909, could we please mark it for identification pending its translation. It might be in as early as tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked for identification as D110.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up P194. It is a map that was admitted as a Prosecution Exhibit. Could we please zoom in on the area of Dobrinja. The area of Dobrinja, it is to the south. A bit more, please. The area of Dobrinja is to the south. Just a bit more, please. Enlarge it a little bit more. If possible, zoom in on this area, where it says "155," the 155th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you see the position of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it. Thank you. Please don't move the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the area of the 155th Brigade, whose commander you were?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where it says "155th," and we see a little flag there, was that your command post? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell exactly on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This marking with the triangle, wasn't that supposed to be the brigade command place? You made these markings. This is your war map, or rather, that of your command. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a map of the 12th Division. If this symbol is used to show the place where brigade command is situated, then I accept your proposition.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The battalion command -- the other little flag, or rather, the triangle, is that where the battalion command was?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are these mortar positions, the mortars of 82-millimetre calibre, between the two flags, and it is supposed to depict a mortar platoon because of the circle just below. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that it was a mortar platoon, but not of 82, but of 60-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that were mortars?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous testimony, I said that we had two to four battalion -- mortars of 60-millimetre calibre per battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The thing next to your command and the one to the right, each of these locations you had between two and four mortars. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they were not close to neither the brigade command nor to the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And this lonesome marking here, isn't that a marking for a mortar of 120-millimetre calibre. Isn't that a sign for a unit which goes forward? Is that a mortar of 120-millimetre calibre?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said previously, we did not have any 100-millimetre [as interpreted] mortars in Dobrinja, but we had 60-millimetre ones and probably this is meant depict that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you are telling us that this marking with the three prongs is not supposed to be a 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling that at Dobrinja there were no 120-millimetre mortars. As I said, we had 60-millimetre mortars. If you are talking about the one mortar of 82-millimetre calibre we had, then this may depict its position, and that's as far as I'm prepared to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the transcript, we have "28-millimetre." I don't know this interpretation. He said something completely different. However, witness, I categorically claim that this is a marking for a 120-millimetre mortar. What have you got to say to that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the situation on the ground. That's why I'm telling you this. Had we had such mortars, these would be -- would have been the markings. But tactically speaking, there was no need for us at Dobrinja to use any mortars other than the 60-millimetre ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How about the three arrows to the right at Mojmilo, are those anti-aircraft pieces --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Anti-armour pieces?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: They were used and there were a number of those. They are to the right of the mortar positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, it could be established first whether they were in the area of responsibility of this gentleman's brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he would say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Witness, it says here "155th Brigade." Yesterday, you explained certain things. We can see your command post. Is this the area of responsibility of the 155th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that I was not interested in these markings. I cannot interpreter them. These three arrows that you showed were beyond the area of responsibility of my brigade, but, rather, that of an adjacent brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But look at the map. The Chamber itself can see, if you look a little by the to the north and up, there's as many as two 120-millimetre mortars in the area of responsibility of the 112th Brigade. I presume that you synchronised your actions through communications system. You knew about these mortars positioned a little bit to the north, didn't you? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, these are the responsibility of other brigades. I didn't know what these other brigades had except for men. I was only interested in my area of responsibility and defence and nothing else, apart from us trying to prevent the breakthrough through the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You acted in concert with the 101st and 102nd Brigade, which later merged into one brigade. Is that correct? And you were its commander?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I could never have -- coordinate any action with any adjacent brigade. If anyone did that, it must have been someone else, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order not to go into all details on this map, can you only confirm that here below 112th, signifies two recoilless guns, and I'm referring to the 112th Mountain Brigade, up there to the north. A little bit above your positions. Were those the emplacement of recoilless guns?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Twice I hear the interpretation and saying the transcript saying "112th Brigade." I only see the 102nd Brigade and the 101st Brigade. If that could be clarified, where that 112th Brigade comes from. I just don't see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The 112th is to the north, on the top left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have been looking at my own e-court system and not at yours. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, before moving on to the issue of recoilless guns, I would like to ask a question of the witness. Mr. Witness, I followed with great care the discussion regarding the types of mortars you had in your brigade. The Defence claimed that you had a 120-millimetre mortars. You, however, said that you only had one calibre, 82 millimetres. Page 9, lines 23 and 24 of the transcript, you said that, tactically, there was no need for mortars other than 60-millimetre mortars. Can you explain this to me? What do you mean by "a tactical need," for only 60-millimetre mortars? Why did you not need 120-millimetre mortars as the Defence claimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area of responsibility of the Dobrinja Brigade, and with regard to our lines and the Serbian lines and the distance between the lines and how they were compact actually, if you have 60-millimetre mortars with a range of around 1.000 millimetres [as interpreted], we couldn't meet our defence requirements. 120-millimetre mortars had range in excess of 3.000 metres; therefore, we did not have any need to target any positions that were not directly putting us at peril.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Should the word in the transcript "if you have 60 metre mortars with a range of around 1.000 millimetres, we couldn't meet our Defence requirements." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. I think the witness said, and because he said he said in chief, that the range of the 60-millimetre mortar would around 1.000 metres, but let the witness confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a technical person, but this "couldn't" -- they are right. Shouldn't it be "could." Logically, he is saying that with 60-millimetre mortars, they "could" meet their defence requirements, so they didn't need anything more. So I'm questioning whether "couldn't" should not be "could." I'm trying to follow the logic of the explanation. May I ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honour. With 60-millimetre mortars, we were able to meet our requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can you just confirm that what is written below 112th Brigade, a little bit to the left, are recoilless guns turned towards Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I told you I know nothing about the marks. If they were there, they were probably there, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not going to ask you to read this map any further. Your commander will be here, and we shall clarify that with him. We have here now another document, DD00-1259, and we have a translation of that document as well. Can we please have this displayed on our monitors. It's been translated. That's a document dated the 12th of August, 1994. It's been written by Van Baal, an UNPROFOR officer, addressed to Jovan Divjak, a deputy commander of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it reads as follows: "Dear General, today, the 12th August at 0515, a mortar shell was shot from the trig point 847-554 to the Serb-held parts of Dobrinje. Once more I want to emphasise that such an act is a flagrant breach of the agreement relating to the total exclusion, signed in February 1994, which should prevent the city of Sarajevo from being shelled." This refers to a shell fired -- fired at Dobrinja. Is it true that you held a section of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, my unit didn't do that. Interestingly, I would like it make a comment, if you allow me, on this document. If this officer wrote this letter, why did he address it to General Divjak? Why didn't he address it to the 1st Corps command or the 12th Division command, but rather he chose to write this letter General Jovan Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it is also important to understand this document, to figure out what that grid refers to, what location. That's where the mortar shell came from, according to Mr. Van Baal. And -- I'm not going to testify, of course, but it need to be made sure where it comes from, whether inside the area of responsibility of this brigade commander or outside the area of responsibility of the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, you told us that Dobrinja was encircled. Isn't it true that Dobrinja was divided into two parts; one was held by the BH army as you indicated on the map, and the other one was held by the VRS. No one was encircled there, but there was rather a separation line. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian forces occupied parts of Dobrinje 4 and Dobrinja 1, as well as part of the airport settlement, and those were the separation lines between one part of Dobrinja and the occupied part of Dobrinja. Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm talking about occupied the parts from which people were expelled. Around 400 people were taken to Kula from the to airport settlement. No one was taken away from Dobrinja 4, but they were rather pushed to the inner part of Dobrinja. And some 200 people were taken away from Dobrinja 1, while the rest were pushed further into the Dobrinja neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have no time to go back to your statement; but in 1992, the first people, except for some few exceptions, were the Serbs. They abandoned their homes and all their belongs back in 1999 [as interpreted], precisely because of the then -- INTERPRETER: Interpreter's correction: 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- precisely because of the then prevailing situation.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one expelled the Serbs from Dobrinja, Mr. Tapuskovic. They followed the instructions given by politicians. They took their things and left Dobrinja, but not all of them. Some of them remained in Dobrinja, and you can check the data about the number of Serbs who remained there. No one was forced to go, and that was the time when there was no conflict yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's stick to the matter at hand. Counsel, you bring forward the document on the screen, and the question is whether the grid position, GR 847-554, is within or without the area of responsibility of the witness. And since you bring forward this document, I suggest that it is on you to show to the Chamber that it is indeed within his area of responsibility, and I kindly ask you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it doesn't say anywhere in this letter that this trig point is in the area of responsibility of the Serbian army. You are asking me to do something which is impossible. In any case, it is clear that this position, with this markings, was in the territory of the BH army. So in that respect, I asked the witness if we have this claim in this letter, and if Dobrinja was closest to the other part of Dobrinja, that is Dobrinja 4, I presume that this shot was fired from the Dobrinja side held by the BH army. And I think that the witness is in the position to answer this. He can tell us where this location exactly was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Shall we hear from the witness or from you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness can answer. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hadzic, what's the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that it wasn't fired from the area of responsibility of our brigade. Even if there had been a mortar, it is technically impossible to fire it, because between the ultimate point of Dobrinja and this point is -- the distance is about 4.000 metres [as interpreted]. So there was no shell fired by the Dobrinja Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the question more precisely is whether, what is it, GR 847-554 is within your area of responsibility. Are you in a position to answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in the area of responsibility of my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we can correct the transcript, it says "4.000 metres;" whereas, the witness says "1.000 metres." It's been recorded "4.000 metres," but the witness says "1.000 metres."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that correct, Witness? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I said that the ultimate point of Dobrinja under our control within -- with respect to Dobrinja 4, the distance is about 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you at least confirm this second part which reads as follows: "It is very disappointing to discover is that especially the BH in the last few days is trying to exploit the situation after the air attack on the 5th of August." Is at least this true? Did you try to abuse and exploit these air attacks on the 5th of August, and to advance or reinforce your positions vis-a-vis the positions of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, when the air strikes started around the area of responsibility of Dobrinja, we rejoiced. We thought and believed that this was the end of the war. Even people rushed out into the street from their flats -- flags [as interpreted]. They were applauding and hailing the aircraft carrying out the air-strikes against the Serbian forces in Dobrinja and Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 5th of August, 1994. I'm not talking about the end of the war, but, rather, the 5th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, if the Serbian forces would attack us, we would defend us, which is a classic example of how our area of responsibility operated. Throughout the war, except for some certain changes, we firmly held to our lines and defended our area of responsibility. If the Serbian forces tried to penetrate our area, we would try to repel them and push them back, and we upheld all the cease-fires 100 per cent because they were in our interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have this document, DD00-1259, be tendered as a Defence exhibit, since we have both versions, English and the B/C/S one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D111, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, the last paragraph of the letter that you have shown on the screen seems to suggest that all the mortars held by the BiH army inside Sarajevo should have been rendered -- or should have been surrendered to the French bat or to the weapon collection point. And this, of course, raises the question whether the BiH army held these mortars, two to four mortars per battalion, in violation of the obligation to surrender all weapons -- all heavy weapons to the weapon collection points. Could you please clarify this with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going ask the witness the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a working map of the 1st Corps from March 1995. Was is entered in these maps signifies active weapons. If that had not been the case, then we would have had exactly the situation described by His Honour Judge Harhoff at the collection points for heavy weapons. Do you deny that on the 3rd of March, a year after the exclusion zone was introduced, these weapons were deployed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, whatever our command signed with international forces was honoured, and we strictly abided by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, I'm putting my question directly to you then. Does this mean that the two to four 60-millimetre mortars that you have told us were in the possession of each of your battalions, that they fell under the minimum limits of the international agreement so that you could told them lawfully. Is that what you are saying? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand your question and precisely so. We abided by whatever was prohibited, and we didn't have any of those things in our possessions. Whatever the command in charge of the 1st Corps signed with international forces, we observed to the letter. Whatever, however, was allowed, we kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, if I -- when I come to the final stage of my cross-examination, I have, however, to raise an objection that was passed on to me by the accused, and I would like to say and ask the witness to explain this. This is not a trig point. These were coordinates, and they were provided by the UN and only they knew what they signified. Therefore, I could not ask the witness anything about it because these coordinates had been provided by the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I was alarmed to hear you say when you come to the final stage of your cross-examination. You are in the final stage of your cross-examination, and you must bring it to an end within two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given the importance of this witness, this directly infringes the right to a fair trial, and I would like you to allow me to show to the witness at least another two documents; but, anyway it is up to you to decide, and the direction of this is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can show the witness the other two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another letter sent by Van Baal; there's no translation of that letter. And its number is DD00-1257.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yet again, on the 13th of August, 1994, Mr. Van Baal writes to General Divjak. So I'm going to read it: "Addressed to the Brigadier-General Jovan Divjak. "General, attached here with, you will find a report by the Sajo airport commander, concerning the shooting on the 11th of August, which was -- directly caused the closure of the airport and delay of flights. "Although you reassured this command that the airport will be freely and used without any hindrance, it seems that the three shots fired from the territory held by the BH army resulted in the air lift, otherwise used to provide for people, to close. Basically, that was an irrational act. "It is obvious that only by taking a very firm and resolute attitude towards such elements can such incidents be prevented in the future. The solutions can be jointly reached between the BH army and UNPROFOR, especially in the period when the airport is in use." My question is as follows: If these bullets or these three shots were fired from ordinary weapons, that could only have come from the positions, because this was not a rocket or anything else, these were rifle bullets, and Dobrinja was under your control. Were those three bullets fired from the area under your direct command?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the airport and the area around it was partly under the respective responsibility of three Bosnian brigades, so any of them could have fired those shots. But the question is why should they be shooting at the aircraft bringing in food and good things. Why should we hinder or hamper anything that was to our benefit? If anybody did shoot, it could not have been from the area of the 155th Brigade or any other brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we have this document, DD00-1257, be marked for identification? I believe that the Prosecution has it, and I don't have a translation because the original is in English. But can we have it marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as D112.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now the last document, even though I have about a dozen more. It's another letter written by Mr. Van Baal to General Divjak, and we have a translation of this document into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems that I did not put it on the list. But may I be permitted to use it anyhow since it has been translated, and I will use this to conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The English version doesn't correspond to the -- to the B/C/S version. It's a different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, the English translation on the left appears to be the English translation of the first document we had discussed at length, which had the grid reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no translation for the document of the 13th; however, I do have the translation of the 15th document. That one was previously marked for identification, and the other one dates the 15th and I have its translation. By your leave, I just wanted to ask for your permission to tender that; and pursuant to your decision, I would conclude with my cross-examination. Perhaps, the witness could read it. I have the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness is reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, he can read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The 15th of August, 1994."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is not French interpretation. Are we going to have French interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is a technical problem, Mr. President. We're going to solve it. Would counsel mind repeating the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I actually asked the witness to read out the document. I have it in English. Perhaps the interpreters could be provided with a copy of that, or it can be put on the ELMO as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, since preference is given to the interpreters, which is fine, for the only English translation, which document are we now talking about? The one I see on the screen has the 13th of August, 1994. Is that the document that we're talking about, or is it a different one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waespi, it has already been marked for identification that. That was not what I was talking about. It is another document dated two days after that, the 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that the document which the witness is now reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, maybe that document should then be placed on the ELMO. Have you read it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be placed on the ELMO so we can hear an interpretation of it, if it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a translation already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the question that you wish to put to the witness about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That fire was opened at an aeroplane immediately or shortly afterwards. And, again, the general was warning the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina not to open fire at aeroplanes, but this one testifies that they indeed continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What paragraph indicates this? I would just ask the interpreter to interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read it out as well. I have it on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have provided the English translation. "On the 15th of August, Brigadier-General Jovan Divjak. Dear General, today on the 15th of August, 1994, at approximately 1.100 hours, an UN aircraft was hit by a single small arms round. Not 24 hours has passed since your representative publicly condemned the practice of shooting at aircraft during yesterday's Sarajevo airport meeting. "Once again irresponsible elements have hit one of our aircraft. It is obvious to me that only through close cooperation between UNPROFOR/air base command and your army and police forces that we can succeed in stopping these attacks." My question is this: Was that bullet fired from your area of responsibility, as it was the only area from which one could open fire at the planes landing at the airport as stated here by Mr. Van Baal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sure that is a misstatement of the situation. The airport has two sides; one is Dobrinja, the other one is Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm convinced that UNPROFOR did its job conscientiously, and they had good foundation for such categorically claims. There is no space for any doubt as to where the fire came from, from which side. They would be familiar with the consequences of that, so perhaps the witness could answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wasn't talking about which side, which forces. I was talking in a geographical sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is a translation in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is the translation? Is there an English translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the English translation on the ELMO? Apparently, it has been given to the interpreters. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The only point I was making was that I didn't dispute that it says here it was the ABiH or come from ABiH. My only objection was to counsel putting to the witness that it must have come from his side, which is Dobrinja, rather than from the Butmir side, where other ABiH air forces were stationed. That was my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we have the letter on the ELMO, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, as I read this letter, it does not say that the shots came from the areas held by the BiH army. At best, the letter suggests that the shots could have come from the BiH army, but there's obviously a possibility that it could also have come from the other side. I see General Van Baal's letter as a warning basically to both sides that they should control so-called irresponsible elements from -- and prevent them from shooting at incoming or outgoing aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please be handed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, are you saying that in the version of document that you have, there's an indication that the shooting came from the BiH army? Because there is no such indication in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let us be clear. They were very clear in their terms used in the previous letter when the three shots were fired. This is yet another warning that they should stop doing what they had done 24 hours before that. In the previous document, it is clearly stated who fired. This one is merely a protest. The other side was never forwarded such a letter. They are yet again protesting with the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear the question and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And putting these two letters together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear the question that you wish to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is this: Both these events, that is rifle or light machine-gun fire, that that fire was fired from Mr. Hadzic's area of responsibility, and I believe the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will use this pointer to try and show you the area of responsibility around the air strip. Let say this is the air strip. One third was in the Serbian hands. This part, from the Serbian forces to the last third, was my area of responsibility and, then, again we have the Serbian forces. And the same goes for the other side of the air strip; Serbian forces, army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then Serbian forces, and both ends of the airport were in the Serbian hands. Had we opened fire at that time, the French Battalion, with which we had excellent cooperation, would have come to warn us. Never have we been warned during that period that someone opened fire from our area of responsibility at aircraft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We thank you. So what is your answer to the question that was put?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not open fire at that aircraft. It could have been anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the document of the 15th of August, I would like to tender it as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit D113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, that now concludes your testimony. We thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I may be excused, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty, you're going to marshall the evidence from the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, and the Prosecution's next witness will be Mr. Per Anton Brennskag.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I would ask to be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit and you may begin, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your name, and by way of introduction tell us what you do for a living.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: My name is Per Brennskag. I couldn't hear the other part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you do for a living.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please say again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you do for a living. What is your employment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Today, I'm retired from my home municipality as chief of administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And before you were chief of administration of your municipality, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I was in the Norwegian army from 1970 to early 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What rank did you hold when you retired from the Norwegian army?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: My rank was lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did your career with the Norwegian army also include service with the United Nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Between what dates, please? When did you begin and when did you end?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I arrived Zagreb early, early 1995, early March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and when -- when did you leave?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I left in 1996. I left Sarajevo mid-September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what was it that you were doing while you were in Sarajevo? What were you doing with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I was an armed military observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, have you on two occasions given statements to investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. Once as far as I remember, 1996; and the last time in October last year, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And since coming to The Hague to give testimony a few days ago, have you had an opportunity to read both of those statements over?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In what language did you read them?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I wrote them in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when you read them, did you find those reports to be accurate summaries of what you had said to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today, would we get the answers that are in those reports?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I move the admission into evidence of 65 ter number 2858, which is the witness' ICTY statement of October 2006, and I also move the admission of 65 ter number 2859, which is the witness's statement from May of 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 2858, the statement of October 2006, will be admitted as Exhibit P345. 65 ter number 2859, the statement of May 1996, will be Exhibit P346.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And may I ask the court officer to bring up the Sarajevo map that has been used many times in these proceedings, 65 ter number 2829.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, while we're waiting for the map to appear, from your service in Bosnia, are you familiar with the term "modified air bomb?"

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What does that term mean to you, or what sort of device does that term describe to you?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: It's normally a ballistic missile put on rockets device, so it will not be ballistic anymore. It could be an air bomb, or up to my knowledge, it also could be an artillery device.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I apologise, Mr. Court Officer, I asked for the map under the wrong 65 ter number. It should have been 2872. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, the modified air bombs that you have been describing, were you ever in a position to see one launched or to see -- excuse me, to see one in flight?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when you see such a thing in flight, how can you tell that it is a modified air bomb and not something else? How can you look at and say, Oh, there goes a modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: It has a smoke tail from the rocket device.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And is there anything else that is distinctive about it?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm not able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, on the monitor in front of you is a map, and I'm going to be asking you some questions about a specific day, the 28th of June of 1995. Were you on duty as a United Nations Military Observer on the 28th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: On the map, can you tell us whereabouts you were on June the 28th of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. I was on the observation post of the Pofalici team. It was located in the area of Vitkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do you see on the map the area of the observation post from the Pofalici team?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to assist the witness, and I'll ask you to mark the observation post with the letters OP for the English "Observation Post."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Put an X at the spot and label it OP, please.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: While you were on doubt at the OP that day, did you see anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. You've testified a few minutes ago that you have seen modified air bombs in flight. Did you have occasion to see a modified air bomb at any time on 28th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And where were you when you saw this modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I was on the OP marked on the map on Vitkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Describe, please, what you saw when you saw this modified air bomb.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I saw it was launched and I saw the flight, and I also pretty sure to see where it was going to have the impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Let's take those up in turn. First of all, where it was launched from. Can you indicate on the map in front of you the area from which you saw this modified air bomb being launched?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Would you take the pen from the usher and mark the area of launch, please.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: This would be a wide area from Ilidza, and I mark it like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. During the time that you were in Sarajevo, did you become familiar with which of the warring factions controlled what territories?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And did you know at the time that you were in Sarajevo who controlled the territory that you have just drawn a circle around in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Who did?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: It was BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the initials "BSA" stand for what, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, just before the break, you had been making some markings on the map, and I just direct your attention to the circle in the lower right, because on the break I was noticing - lower left, excuse me - that there was a river running through that circle. Were you able to tell from which side of that river the air bomb was launched on the 28th of June, or can you not be more precise than the circle?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Taken in consideration that it was 12 years ago and I don't have the exact report from that time, I don't want to be more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's fair enough, thank you. Describe the flight of this air bomb, please.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you want me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm just asking to you tell us in words, no need to mark on the map and I apologise for not being clear, just tell us in words what you saw when this air bomb flew through the air. What did its flight look like?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Well, in the first time of the flight when the rocket engine was on, it's like a striped mark on the air; and afterwards when the motor is off or burned out, it's not possible to see, if you are not lucky to see, the shell until it's -- having its impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, you said in your last answer that --

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sorry. I hadn't turned my microphone on; I have now. You said in your last answer that it was a straight mark on the sky. You have seen -- or have you seen artillery shells in flight during your military career?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I have seen mortar shells during exercise when they are -- have a very high altitude, and you have everything under control. You can see a black mark on the sky going up and going down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is there anything different about -- between the flight of a mortar shell and the flight of a modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. If you are not lucky to look directly at where the mortar or the artillery is launched, you can't see anything. If you are lucky to look directly look at it, you can see the smoke from -- from the weapon, but just short.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was trying to ask was is there something different between a modified air bomb, on the one hand, and an artillery shell or a mortar shell, on the other hand, about the kind of path that they make when they are travelling through the sky. Do you understand that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I understand. Mortar or an artillery shell have a ballistic way. The rocket has not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you say "a ballistic way," is it possible for you to describe a bit more fully what you mean by "ballistic way"?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: A mortar or an artillery shell don't have any other way of putting themselves through the air than from the Howitzer or from the motor. But the rocket gives - what should I say in English? - gives it power through the air after leaving the Howitzer or the mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How many times during your service in Sarajevo, did you see modified air bomb launches, approximately? I know it's been some years.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Approximately, four or five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And were you able to, by what you saw, know that you were looking at a modified air bomb launch rather than artillery or mortar or something else?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: After the first time, you are very certain what you are -- the difference between mortars, artillery, and modified air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let's go back to the 28th of June then. After you saw this launch, did you observe an impact of a modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I saw an impact, yes, and it must be the modified air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Where did you see that impact?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: The impact was in the so-called TV building in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the position of the TV building; and if so, could you mark that on the map with an X and labelling it "TV?"

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. I know where the TV building is in Sarajevo, and I mark it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if you could just label that "TV," please.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you said a minute or two ago, "it must have been the air bomb that impacted the TV building," what are your reasons for making that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: The conclusion comes to me because of what I saw was launched and the impact just after I couldn't see the rocket smoke anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Now, during your service in Sarajevo, did you ever meet a Danish colleague, an UNMO named Thomas Hansen.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I can't remember the name, but for sure I could have met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. But no recollection as you sit here today.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was that officer, Mr. Hansen, ever at the Pofalici OP, where you've testified you were on duty on the 28th of June?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: You mean the Vitkovac OP?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: As far as I know, I have never seen Hansen on the Vitkovac, but for sure he could have been there when I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you were not there, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not clear to me what the witness is saying. Do you know Mr. Hansen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know Mr. Hansen. I could have met him, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's the point I'm trying to elicit, Mr. President. I am going somewhere with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay, let's see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 00536, please. Oh, I'm sorry. Yes, could I tender the map as marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P347, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But I have a problem with the list of documents that was supposed -- that will be used with this witness. I only have three documents on the list and the map. I didn't raise any objection because I have the same map on my own list, but I really do not know what documents we're talking about. I don't think they were supposed to be used today by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: May I respond, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The document I have just called for is Captain Hansen's special report of the 29th of June, and it is on the Defence list which was released to me at the beginning of the witness's direct examination. It is not on the Prosecution's list of exhibits; however, it is it on the Defence list of exists. It is UNMO HQ Sector Sarajevo special report on impact on TV building, I believe, it is cell number 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, do you see an United Nations report in English on the left-hand side of the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do you see that this is prepared by a Captain T. Hansen?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if I might ask the court officer to go to the second page of this document, in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Brennskag, I'm going to direct your attention to the second-to-the last paragraph in Mr. Hansen's report. I will read it out in English. "The UNMO team that normally man OP4 that looks into the area was taking cover in the shelter because of shelling at the time of the incident, so no information is available from the OP." Have I read that accurately?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The reference there is to "OP4," and in your testimony you have spoken about the Pofalici or the Vitkovac OP. What is the relationship between OP4 and the Vitkovac OP that you have been -- I'm sorry, I see that is confusing you. The Vitkovac OP, did it have a number?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. It had OP4 and was the OP for the Pofalici team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Going back to Captain Hansen's report, were you in fact taking shelter at the time that this air bomb was launched, as it says in this report?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Was there a shelter at OP4?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: It was normally a family house with a basement for potatoes and vegetables, and this is what they called the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Had you ever taken shelter during your time at OP4?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you ever tell Captain Hansen that you were taking shelter at the time of this air bomb incident regarding the TV tower?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Not as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, lastly, this paragraph that we've been concentrating on for the past few minutes, is it in your opinion correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I would not speculate in the report. For me, it's looks some incorrect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Was there anyone else on duty with you at OP4 that day when you made these observations?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. We were always two observers on the OP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Had the other observer taken shelter?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And who was the other observer?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm not able to remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, lastly, if we could go back to the map that we had on the screen, I understand it will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can he say how many soldiers were in OP4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, can you tell us how many UNMOs were in OP4.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, do you mean by that two at any given time were on duty, or maybe two out of six or two out of eight, or what have you, were on duty. How big was the team from which those two came?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: The teams normally was eight or nine observers. On the OP, there were only two at each time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And did he say who those two were whether he knew those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: He was one, and he cannot recall the name of his colleague, given that it has been ten years. But there was a second with him that day, and I believe his testimony was neither one of them had taken shelter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it possible that some other members of the UNMO team of eight might have taken shelter there without your knowing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why would you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the Pofalici team had their accommodation fairly long away from the OP. So the OP just consisted of the house and always two UNMOs when we were able to be at the OP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: OP stands for what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Observation post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Observation post, and this house was the observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The house was the observation post; the upper floor of the house was the observation post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And is that where you were at the time of the -- the flight of this air bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I just wonder if it's possible to have the marked map put back up. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, in front of you is the map that you marked a little bit earlier - it's now in evidence - did you look at Captain Hansen's report before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. I was shown the report for two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in that report there is a map grid reference; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The map that is on the screen does not have the numbers that are necessary to plot a map grid reference. Am I correct in that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Were you able to work out on this map that is on the monitor where a particular map reference point would be?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you describe to Their Honours how you went about figuring out where a map reference point would be, given that this map does not have the necessary numbers.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. I used the map with a grid reference and found where the -- the spot were and compared it to this map shown on the screen, and it's fairly no problems to know where it is on this grid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to -- since I don't want to take this map off the screen, I'm going to read to you a portion of Captain Hansen' report. This is one that contains the map grid reference. "Heard and saw an outgoing projectile across the parking place and road from grid BP 866-587." That -- you were able to plot that grid on the map on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, fairly accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you please mark that spot with an X; and then I'll ask you to label that X, "TH" for Thomas Hansen.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you have any opinion as to the feasibility of launching a modified air bomb from the spot labeled "TH" towards the TV tower or at the TV tower?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I have no education how they launched the improvised air bombs. But as far as I can recall, this would be a big problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Why would it be a big problem, Mr. Brennskag?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: It's the distances that directly hit, directly sight, a very short distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And why is it -- I'm sorry. I'm not entirely clear. Why is it a big problem to fire a modified air bomb at a target that is a relatively short distance away?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: As I said, I have no education about how to fire it. But for me, I think it would be a big problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher. Thank you. We're finished with marking the map. Your Honour, I'll tender the second version of the marked map as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It says that he thinks it would be a big problem. Why do you think it would be a big problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can't answer it. Because, as you say, you -- you have, as you said in your own words, no education about how who fire it. Are you able to tell us what that area is that you marked "TH"? What is the locality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's near the railroad and it's a main road on the knot of the railroad, and there are some factory buildings or railroad buildings very close to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the name of the -- the district or the village or the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't -- I can't tell you, sir. On the map, it's Alipasin Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us the distance between the point marked "TH" and the TV tower that was hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Approximately, about 500 metres or slightly a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: May I tender the map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P348, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, we're through with marking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Since you are still examining in chief, I'm putting my question through you, which I think is the correct thing to do, and I want you to put the question to the witness so that the Chamber can understand what it is the witness saw. What he has told us was that he saw a modified air bomb being launched from the circle in the Ilidza area, and then, as I understood it, in the straight line to the TV building. And I would like you to ask the witness to confirm that this is what he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: A couple of questions, Mr. Brennskag. Just would you tell the Chamber again in as much as detail as possible, please, what you saw of this modified air bomb -- what you observed - I don't want to limit it to "saw," because you may have heard things or what have you - what you observed of this modified air bomb from launch to impact.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I saw a modified air bomb launched from the Ilidza area towards PTT building, TV building, and I saw the rocket smoke and just afterwards an impact in the TV building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And was it a straight line from the launching point to the impact point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So the implication of your answer is that the modified air bomb that you saw could not have passed over the point identified by Captain Hansen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, I just want it turn back for a moment or two to this question. When we asked why this would be a big problem, you said partly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sorry, Mr. Prosecutor. I just want to make sure of one thing. Did the witness himself reach a conclusion, whatever it may have been, as to the armed group that launched the bomb, because in his report he said that the modified air bomb left from the Ilidza zone. However, did he manage to reach a conclusion as to who launched the bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was launched from the BSA area, Bosnian Serb army area, held area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's all I wanted to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just a couple of more questions, Mr. Brennskag, and then we will be finished.
