A few minutes ago you were answering the question about why it would be a big problem to launch this air bomb from the spot marked "TH" to hit the spot marked TV, and you said a couple of different things. You said that you didn't have knowledge of how these things were launched, but at one point you also said it was too short. When you saw four or five air bombs being launched, as you've testified you saw during your time in Sarajevo, can you describe the kind of flight path that you observed on those four or five occasions?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I'll try. They were launched in a, let's say, 45 degrees and had a fairly long path. I'm not sure if I'm answering you correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let me -- let me put it this way: If an air bomb was launched from the spot marked "TH," which at least on my version just went off the screen. But if it was launched from the "TH" point in the direction of the TV point, when it reached the TV point, what would such an air bomb be doing, if it acted like the other four or five that you saw? That was long question. Do you understand what I'm asking?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I understand. The launch must have been horizontal, horizontal, if that is the correct English word. So it would go 90 degrees towards the wall or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you ever observe an air bomb launched horizontally of the four or five that you saw?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You testified a moment ago that they went up at about a 45 degree angle. Was that true of all four or five of them?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, fairly correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, lastly, did you ever see modified air bombs on the Bosnian Muslim side of the confrontation lines? I mean unfired - I know you investigated and saw them after they had landed - but unfired air bombs on the Bosnian Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I have never seen unfired modified air bombs on either of the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Oh. And the air bomb incidents that you -- did you investigate air bomb incidents during your time as a military observer?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And were those incidents were the impacts on the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Serb side of the lines?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: On the BiH side, the Bosnian Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I am Branislava Isailovic, a lawyer at the Paris Bar, and I defend the accused General Dragomir Milosevic. First of all, Mr. President, I would like to address the Chamber for to you decide on the use of documents offered during examination-in-chief. Indeed, the Prosecutor believes he is entitled to use documents offered by the Defence, and he wants to use them during examination-in-chief. So I would like you to decide, is this proper, is it in keeping with the rules or not, before I start with my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not an objection that you raised at the time. Why didn't you raise that objection at the time when it was being tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I waited because I didn't want to interrupt the examination-in-chief. I did raise an objection. I said that it was not a document on the list, and the Prosecutor answered that the document was part of the Defence list, which is true. Therefore, I waited until now and as for future reference, because I believe this is a relevant issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but you may be caught by leges. Let me hear from the Prosecutor on this technical point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, in general, Mr. President, we will always put on our list all of the documents that we intend to use. This, I trust, will be an exception. The document was on the Defence list. I understood Ms. Isailovic's objection at the time to be founded on the grounds of unfair prejudice, and therefore my response that it was on the Defence list was meant to say that, Well, this is a document with which the Defence may be expected to be familiar. I certainly would have led the evidence with or without the document regarding the launching sites and so forth. So I don't know that even had the submission been made and been accepted by the Chamber, it may have made the chief a little by the more awkward and a little by the longer. But I don't know that there would have been any more substantive effect than that. But, as I say, this was an exception, given that the document did appear on the Defence list; and, as I say, I perhaps misunderstood counsel for the Defence at the time. I was responding to what I perceived be an objection premised upon unfair prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about their position of principle in proceedings of this kind? Why shouldn't a party be able to use a document that is on the exhibit list of another side? I'm not sure why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I confess that I'm not sure why not either, Your Honour. If the --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, because -- may I -- may I make my submissions? First of all, the Defence is under the obligation to disclose its list when the witness is going to start his or her examination. So the Prosecutor is not supposed to know the Defence exhibits beforehand; and to say that anyway, it's in the list, in the Defence list, that is not an argument because it is an erroneous argument. It may be true for us, for us as, in the future, also for the Prosecution. This is true for the cross-examining party, because 48 hours beforehand I'm aware of the Prosecutor' list. So I do not have in my list the documents that the Prosecutor is going to use in his list because any way I could, and I do this systematically. In my own list, I do mention this just to warn them of my interest in all these documents. So here we found ourselves in a situation in which the Prosecutor is asking us to protect the Prosecution's rights to allow them to use documents of the Defence for examination-in-chief without prior warning. Because, you see, Mr. President, Your Honours, I get prepared as we do any Defence counsel, based on what is going to be put forward in the examination-in-chief, and that is the way I organise my cross-examination, in addition to other documents for my own case. So here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. But what prejudice would you suffer, because this document was on your list. So that, in any event, you have a familiarity with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, fortunately it is the case now, but in the future it could be different. This is why I'm interested in your opinion in principle; for instance, I was interested in this and I prepared beforehand whilst this document was not part of the Prosecution list. I, too, am interested in the subject. That is why I have it in my list. Let us not forget that this witness is a 92 ter witness. We had two lengthy prior statements, including a lot of details, many chapters still to come. So we're now focussing only on those statements, or at least we -- we did not say a word on the statements but there was an investigation. Just as well I got prepared because this is what I would do as well. But I want to avoid this in the future. That's why I would like to know what you think. Does the Prosecutor -- or is he under the obligation of disclosing or indicating to the Defence which are the documents he is planning to use during examination-in-chief or not? I just want to know to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I think the answer has to do with an examination of the nature of the proceedings here. The proceedings are essential adversarial; but even in the classical adversarial system, I'm not sure that an objection of this kind would be upheld. And it seems to me that over the years the strict adversarial procedure here has been modified with the adoption of many features from the inquisitorial system. Because this wouldn't arise in the system with which you are familiar in Paris. This issue wouldn't arise at all, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we're talking about the inquisitorial system which is originally mine mean and also that of the accused. We have the investigating judge as an institution; therefore, everything that is in the file is in the trial record. So when I appear before you, everybody knows everything. There is no surprise. We have the file and the file has been established by the investigating judge, and it's followed to the letter. It's not up to any party. Even if parties have suggestions, they must have put them to the investigating judge. They must ask for various steps to be taken; and if the court insists, if you your own witnesses, you have to forewarn the court. I think the time-period is one week ahead of the hearing, so everyone knows everything once you appear in court. So I believe that this is precisely where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, regrettably, the Chamber is not with you on this point. I had described it as a technical point, because what -- that may be a little unfair. You are relying on the practical procedures, which the Chamber itself had set out and which we expect to be followed. But those procedures are more of guidance than rules, and it is always within the discretion of the Chamber to deviate from it if it considers that doing would advance the interests of the case that we are trying. And I would not expect the Prosecutor to be doing this frequently; but in this case, the Chamber is quite prepared to allow him to utilise the document, even though it was not on his list, and for that reason to that extent had you no forewarning of it. But we allow on the basis that it was on your list. Therefore, we cannot see what prejudice you would suffer, because would you have developed a familiarity with it, sufficient to conduct your examination or to react to anything that the Prosecutor led in examination-in-chief. So we'll allow it. But it is not to be taken as meaning that the guidelines which we set have no value. They do have value, and we expect both parties to adhere to them, subject to the qualifications we have set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President. JUDGE ROBINSON Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I don't mean to unnecessarily prolong this, but I do I think it is important for me to put one or two things on the record in case this should ever be looked at by a different Chamber. I want it to be of record that we did file a proofing note. Your Honours have not seen it, but the Defence did. The contents of the proofing were exclusively about the observations from OP4 on the 28th of June, of 1995. And I'll also note for the record - and the transcript is page 21 and 22 of the last witness, Mr. Hadzihasanovic - that the last document which Mr. Tapuskovic used was also not on his list, and there was no objection from the Prosecution. That being said, I take Your Honours point, and that is why I described it as an exception, I think, three or four times. This is not something to made a habit of. We understand the Chamber's guidelines, and we, I think, have followed them very, very well. This was one exception, and I believe it was justified by the fact that, as we have said, it was on the Defence list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is this proofing note that you filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It's a short note, Your Honour. If anything -- if we meet with a witness and something is -- during proofing that we feel need to be disclosed, then we type up what we call an information report and we send it by e-mail to counsel for the Defence. And in this case, after meeting with Mr. Brennskag, I typed up such a note, and I sent it to the Defence through the case manager and it concerned exclusively the events of 28th June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you say "filed," you mean that you sent it to the Defence, not through the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I used the term too loosely, but it concerned the did Captain Hansen ever talk to you about being under shelter. That was the subject of the nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you're saying that any event the Defence did have some warning of this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That is not to be taken as an excuse for not having the document on the list but again it was an exception, and in this case I believe a harmless one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one thing. Mr. Docherty said something after your ruling. Can I use the same right as Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes. But I closed the issue, but very briefly. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So putting documents on a list, it is hard for the Chamber, not only for the Defence but also for the Chamber, because you also get the list of the documents that will be used by both parties. We -- systemically, we send to the Prosecution and to the Chamber. And regarding this report, I also placed it on my own list because I plan to use it. And that way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I have already ruled on it, and you're just regurgitating arguments that we have already heard. Please proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Okay. To save time, I prepared the two statements that have already been tendered by the Prosecution, and I have hard copies because I believe it will be easier to use hard copies on the screen. I have four copies. Prosecution confirmed they already have their own hard copy. So I have three copies for the Judges and one for the witness, and they're -- these are statements that are in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So first, I would like, Mr. Witness, to start with the map we have on screen, number 348. I think this map is still on the screen. Witness, please, on this map with a blue pen - and I would like the usher to please help the witness - could you please draw the trajectory that you observed from where you were in your OP; the flight path, please, on the day that the impact actually occurred. Can you please draw the flight path.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This is the flight path, but I don't think you get the target here. So maybe we should re -- re-draw the flight path because you said that the target was the TV building, and the TV building is on the map next to the cross that you put. And, obviously, the flight path does not end on the TV building. Do you see what I mean? Do you see the TV building on this map, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, and I understand what you mean. Maybe my drawing is a little bit too uncorrect. Okay. It's 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But what you observed from OP4 is a flight path that was of that distance?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what exactly did you see, except for the white smoke trail?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Because of the smoke trail, I could clearly see from where it would -- it was launched, and I could see a part of the flight path because of the smoke from the rocket; and just afterwards, I saw the impact in the TV building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But my question was whether you saw anything else other than this white smoke trail.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you confirmed the content of the two statements you made on May 2nd, 1996 and October 25th and 26th, 2006. I'm sure that you remember that you confirmed the content of these statements. Could you please answer with a yes or no, so that it can be noted on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please take your 2006 statement and find page 5, paragraph 28. And please tell me what this paragraph means to you.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: It means the same as I tried to explain. I watched the smoke of the trail almost all the way, but I didn't see the smoke -- or the smoke from the rocket was not all the way down to the TV building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that that's what you are reading in paragraph 28?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. The --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see the word "smoke"?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No. I mean the "smoke" when I was stating I watched it almost all the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, unfortunately, I don't speak English but what is written here is "I watched it." "It" is the projectile rather than the smoke, because the word "smoke" is not in your statement, or maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I have no other answer other than I mean that I saw the smoke from the projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think what the counsel would want you to explain is why you didn't say that when you gave your statement, because there's no reference to any smoke in paragraph 28.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please keep this paragraph on hand, and take the statement of 1996. Unfortunately, the paragraphs are not marked here, but I'm looking at page 4 in this statement in the middle of the page, about in the middle of the first -- of this statement. "[In English] The projectile was launched from the Ilidza area, sure from VRS-held territory. I can be sure about this because I know from where the projectile was launched." [Interpretation] That's all you said. So, Witness, please, can we agree to say that your knowledge of the incident increased greatly after seeing the Prosecutor on March 7, 2007? Is it true to say that? Is it fair to say to say that?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, did you make a report on what you say that day?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This is extremely interesting, what happened on the TV building. At first, it didn't sound like it was going to be interesting, but it's getting more and more interesting. So let's talk about Captain Hansen, if you allow me. You don't remember his name. You might have seen him somewhere. I think that's as far as it goes.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, does the name Mibub Il Alem [phoen], a lieutenant-colonel, ring a bell. I believe his name is Ul Alem [phoen].

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What about -- I think I'm going spell is out for the transcript, S-u-n-d-q-u-e-s-t, it would be a major.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What about Tarak Alam [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I know a name Tarak, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, your observation post was OP4, right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you knew that there was an UNMO HQ located in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where that HQ was located?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: It was located in the former television -- no, telephone and -- or we wall the PTT building, Post and Telephone building, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, so there was a HQ. There were officers working in that HQ. I'm sure you know that?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever encounter these people in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Of course, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo, did you ever have to write reports and hand them over to the people working in the HQ?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, but not during my time in the Pofalici team. I was not a senior then. So I didn't deliver reports when I was in the Pofalici team.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us today the name of this senior person who wrote those reports and handed them over to the officers in the HQ of UNMOs in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Among the members of your team at OP4, you're saying that there was a person, your senior manager or something, who went to the PTT building to give the reports. Could you tell us the name of your senior officer in the Pofalici team?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I don't have the names at remembering here. It was different senior officers, at least two times changing, while I was in the Pofalici team.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the period -- the day -- the period of June 28. I think you started with this position early in June. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Earlier in June, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you leave that position, that team?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Let me think. Last part of August, yeah. Maybe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So that's a three-month period?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Who was -- who were the senior officers who contacted the HQ at the beginning of your stay in the Pofalici team ?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have to correct myself, because I left Sarajevo in the middle part of September, so it must have been earlier than the last part of August that I left the team.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Could you please ask the question -- the last question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when exactly did you stay in OP4? Could you give us the dates.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: We were talking about the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Reformulate everything. You arrived on June 2nd at OP4. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No. I arrived at Pofalici team at around the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. And you left -- left it before August. Is that what you answered?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No. I said I left it before the late part of August, so maybe in the middle part of August. I'm not sure of the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. So it's a short period of time. We're talking about two and a half months. Did your senior officer who was in charge of communication of the HQ change over that two-month period?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm not sure of your question. The senior officer or the team when they were working were in contact with the UNMO HQ in the PTT building very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, yourself, personally when you had something to say, when you had observed something, who did you talk to? Who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: It depended on what work we were on. When we were on the OP, we normally reported by radio immediately. If not, it was made a statement by the senior on the observation post when we left the OP and then went to the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So regarding June 28, 1995, according to your memory, did you tell what you have just explained to us here in this courtroom to anyone?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: As far as I know today, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And this person that you told it to, was it a person who was supposed to report this information to the HQ?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Today, yes, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: When you started testifying this morning, on page 34 in today's transcript, line 25, you mentioned a report. You said - I'm not quoting exactly - but you said: "I don't have the report with me." Were you thinking of a very specific report that someone might have drafted after having learned from you what you had seen on June 28, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that, so I can't answer you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't understand why you said you have no knowledge. What the counsel is saying is that in your earlier testimony you had mentioned a report, and she wanted more information about the report. Can you -- do you remember that, when you were being questioned by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not make any written report about the incident, and I suppose that it was made a report, but I have never seen the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you have been required to make a report in the normal course of your duties about this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Normally, yes. But I did not make the written report, and I have not seen the report, until I saw the report from the UNMO HQ two days ago made by the Officer Hansen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do I understand then that you did make an oral report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How? Was that by your radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Either by the radio or when I was in PTT building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On what day would that have been? The same day as the incident or after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have been the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, was it sufficient just to make a radio report? I imagine that seeing an air bomb was something that didn't happen often. It was pretty novel for an UNMO. Don't you think that would have deserved to be specifically reported in a specific way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should have been, but I'm not sure if this happened at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So maybe we can refresh your memory. Because after what happened that day, a huge investigation was launched within the UNMOs. So is that helping you refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. I know it was an investigation at the TV building because of the shelling. I was not a part of the investigation, and I am not sure if there were any UNMOs or other UN units who did the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, but I think we're not talking about the same thing. Could you please look at paragraph 16 in the statement you gave on October 2006.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Excuse me, did you say paragraph 16?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] 16. [Interpretation] Yes, 16.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: From my statement 26th October 2006?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a couple of names here that drew my attention; Captain Nermen and Captain Edbu. Well, there's three names; there's also Captain Goro. Do you see these three names? I don't think you had the best of times with these people. This is not the best memory that you have of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I -- I know the names, yes, and I was working -- this was our liaison officer officers from the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement, you say that these people placed restrictions on you. Do you see that in the statement, in paragraph 16?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So I'd like to know exactly how they placed restrictions on you. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. They told us where we were not allowed to go, either on investigations or to -- to check if something had happened, and we had to -- not to go there, where they told you we were not allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you're not the first UNMO here telling us about these restrictions, so could you tell -- tell us exactly how you were restricted from doing whatever?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes, I'll try. We were supposed to have freedom of movement, but we were always to announce in advance where we intended to go. Normally, this was a message through the liaison officers, and then if they were -- they could put restrictions on us. And, normally, as I stated, they called it safety measures for ourselves for our own safety. That was the reason they said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What kind of relationship did you have with these liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them had their office in the PTT building, so we had to meet them sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But what -- what kind of relationship did you have with them? Did you get along with them? Was it a good relationship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that they were officers, and we had a normal professional officers' relationship. So we had a good talk when we were talking together. No hostilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Notwithstanding the restrictions they placed on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I believe it was their job to hand over to us their orders from the their subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, you know, I'm always thinking in legal terms. But, you know, when there's a rule, if you transgress the rule, there is always a sanction. So according to you, what could have been the sanction if someone was not obeying the restrictions?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I would not speculate on that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Personally, you always obeyed the rule.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't have the arm; they had the arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you that question. So they were armed on top of everything?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Normally, in the army they are armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, earlier, when I asked you about the investigation, I was not talking about the investigation after the incident with the crater analysis and so on. All this has been done, I know. But I was talking about an investigation conducted within your institution, the-- within the UNMO institution, investigation among different officers after June 28th. I think this investigation lasted a week. Do you have any recollection of this inquiry, of this internal inquiry, at the centre of which was Captain Hansen?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I -- as far as I remember, I was not a part of this internal investigation. And I didn't -- and today I don't remember if it was an internal investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, we'll adjourn now for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you continue, Ms. Isailovic, I'll just give a decision on the Prosecution's partly confidential motion for protective measures for witnesses W-32, W-57, and W-95. In that motion, the Prosecution requested that each witness be assigned a pseudonym, be allowed to testify with image distortion, and that W-57, in addition, be allowed to testify with voice distortion. The Prosecution attached a confidential Annex setting out the circumstances supporting the requests for protective measures. The Defence did not respond to the motion, but the Defence has on certainly occasions indicated that as a matter of principle, it does not object to the granting of protective measures, so long as such measures do not completely exclude the public. In light of all the circumstances, including the submissions made by the Prosecution and the contents of the Annex and also in light of the relative provisions of the statute and its Rules, the Chamber grants the motion. Please continue, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, we mentioned this internal investigation of which you say you were not a part of; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I was not a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Were there possibly rumours circulating among the UNMO soldiers, since - how shall I put it? - some kind of force was used against your members?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No, not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that among the officers in the UNMO HQ, there was an officer in charge of relationships with the PO teams?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No, I only know about the liaison officer. I called the liaison officer -- offices in the PTT building. I don't remember and I don't understand what you are meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What I mean is this: Among the UNMO people working in the headquarters, there was somebody who was in charge of giving instructions to the people manning the POs, including yours. Is that right? A kind of operational officer.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It was an operational officer in the UNMO HQ, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know his name by any chance?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: For two days ago, I wrote a statement from 1995 where it was stated that Hansen was the operational officer, but I couldn't remember it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let us return to what you saw on that day. It can be said today that all you saw was this white smoke, the white trail of smoke?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: More specifically, you saw the white trail of smoke coming from a specific direction; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, did you see only one white smoke trail?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was more shelling that day, but I can't remember more than one smoke trail.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at what time you saw the white trail of smoke?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Not -- no. Not until I saw the HQ statement of the 29th of June, where it was said that it was in the morning, but I couldn't myself remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is your evidence that you did not remember the time when you saw the white trail of smoke until you saw the HQ statement of the 29th, which said it was in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statement said it was, I think it was 9.20 in the morning, and that of course I couldn't remember before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is that you can't remember? That it occurred in the morning or the time at which it occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In which time of the day it occurred. If it was 9.00, 10.00, 11.00, I simply couldn't rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Going in the same direction, what statement are you speaking of? When did you state that it was at 9.20?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: When I saw the report from the UNMO HQ two days ago, it was dated 9.20, and this is not my remembrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So here before the Chamber, it can be said that in the two statements used here you never made any mention of the exact time when you saw the bomb as it was launched from Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I can't remember that I have stated the exact time. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And I do take note of this. In your statements, there's no mention of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the map, P348. I started annotating or marking with you. I want to keep it, or save it, please, Mr. Registrar. Mr. President, I'd like it tender this map into evidence with the additional marking made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D114, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask my case manager to display 65 ter document 297.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, have a look at your statement made in 1996, and please go to page 3, third paragraph. Did you find the paragraph? It starts with: "We could see."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned the air bombs that were launched from the VRS-held territory. Further on, you speak about mortars which you saw fired from the Bosnian government's side. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Sorry, could you please say again?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The second sentence in this paragraph starts with the following words: "What concerns what I could see."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Further on, you state that close to your OP there was an ABiH T55 tank, and you say that you never say it fired -- or fire?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This is my first question. Did you always keep an eye on this tank?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No. But what I say, I never saw it being firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now zoom in to enlarge the map so as to see the central part of it. Could we take it down a little, scroll it down, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You, as an officer, can you find your way on this military map?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. It's a little by the unclear on the screen, but of course I can find my way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could we scroll it down a little and then enlarge the part where we see 102. Yes, the part that is darker.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise -- can you see Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Around the word "Sarajevo," can you see various markings?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you maybe see one mention indicating heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: It's unclear for me. Is it possible to scroll it more down, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, scroll it down, but also zoom in just to enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Look at these markings, the various signs on this -- or icons on this map.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: What kind of marking do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I mean all these markings. Among them can you find any showing the positions of heavy weapons, mortars, tanks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with those markings, so I can't say for sure if -- if I have a pen, I could --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm not certain because I'm not familiar with the -- with this kind of military markings. But over here it's stated "155," and I'm not sure if this is a 155 military -- artillery. So I can't say. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's move on. In your prior statement, in paragraph 24 to start with, this is the statement you made in 2006 where the various paragraphs are numbered. The first words of that paragraph are: "The Bosnians often fired."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: 24. Indeed, you speak of mortars here that were positioned close to the -- or near the PTT building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of that paragraph, you say this: "[In English] Military position within civilians areas, which is something they should not have done."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As an officer, could you be more specific. What does this mean to you?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: It means to me, if you, for example, establish a smaller HQ in a flat or a basement where civilian people are living, I would not be allowed to do that, and I should not do that. That's what I mean here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: During your tour in Sarajevo, in the part of the territory held by the ABiH, did you realise there was such positions of HQ in civilian buildings or as you say here in this paragraph that there were mortars positioned near the PTT building? Were you able to see, to observe that?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I was able to see firing from -- mortars from this car junkyard.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In the last sentence of paragraph 24, which military positions specifically are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm talking about small HQs. That's what I remember. That I was -- when I was stating this, it is fairly close to where people are living.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So between these HQs, as you say, were there soldiers that would circulate between them?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I don't understand what you are meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Military personnel, ABiH soldiers, say, would they go to these HQs?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge, but I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: During your tour of service, as of the 2nd of June, were you able to observe the presence of soldiers in the centre of Sarajevo, in the part that was held by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do you mean soldiers in uniform or soldiers battling or in positions?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you know what a soldier is. A soldier, in my view, is somebody carrying a weapon. He may not necessarily be wearing a uniform, but uniform, weapons, anything that is -- shows that a person is not a civilian individual.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. During my time in Sarajevo, I saw several times soldiers in uniform, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall a time during your mission, so starting on the 2nd of June, and that would be around the 15th of June, do you recall intense military activities throughout the territory of Sarajevo held by the ABiH, but also on the territory held by the VRS, or BSA?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the date. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Still, around that time, in that period from the 2nd of June until, as we established, mid-August 1995, was that a period of more intense military activities?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: It escalated and the military activity was very high up to the middle part of August, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember that during that period UNMOs were not authorised to go on their own initiative to the Sarajevo hospitals or in that part of Sarajevo that was controlled by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, go to your first statement, the one made in 1996. The paragraphs are not numbered. That is towards the end of page 3. We're going to speak about this: I quote: "I investigated two impacts of these modified air bombs. [In English] We were not allowed to go to the hospital."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did that happen only once? Were you not allowed to go to the hospital only once?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I don't remember, but this special occasion I remember because I was a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Witness. Let us speak about this incident that occurred on the 22nd of June, 1995, in the Geteova Street. This is what you said. Do you remember the name of that street?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I'm not sure the name of the street, but it's in the vicinity of Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a more specific recollection of this incident?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. I was not on OP that day, so me and I think two of my colleagues were designated to investigate the impact in Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you speak about this incident in both statements. We've just seen this in the first statement, and now this has jogged your memory. Your second statement in paragraph 25, there's also reference to this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before moving to the second statement, could the witness tell us why he was not authorised to go to hospitals. That's page 3 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please. Counsel, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the question put by Judge Mindua. So in your view, and as far as you recall, what was the reason: Why weren't you able to visit hospitals?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: At that incident, we were not allowed to go to the hospital as far as I know, and I don't know why, and I don't know the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So who told you not to go there?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was the local Sarajevo police who were also investigating the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is it the members of this local police who forebade you to go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: As far as I know today, I think it was the local police at the incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, I know this -- this dates back a long time, but do you remember the moment you arrived on site? First question: Did anyone call you there?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. We were called to do the investigation by the UNMO HQ.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived on the site, do you recall anything -- or rather, do you recall the people that you might have seen on the site?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: When I arrived the site, they were just about to take away a girl under a blanket and I remember her father. He was very upset.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember the people who carried that little girl under the blanket?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you -- did you see what was under the blanket, or did you just see the blanket that was covering the body?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No. I saw it was a young girl.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that you were not allowed to take photographs on the site. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, that day, did you see anyone else taking photographs on site?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. The Sarajevo police, who made also a parallel investigation, had photo on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the marks that this air bomb might have left on site?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: On the -- on the road, asphalt road or tarmac road.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you see the marks of the impact on the wall of the building that was located close to that impact site that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And after your investigation on the site, you noted that this bomb that fell and left markings on the -- in the asphalt definitely killed people who were in the building. That was the result of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No, not the result of our investigation. We investigated the impact on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But as a person involved in the investigation, do you find it feasible that the shrapnel of a bomb that would have fell outside a building would kill people that would be inside a building located close to the first impact site?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I object to the question that was just put as misstating the witness's answer. The sequence of questions was: Did your investigation show that people were killed inside the building; the answer was no. And then as though the answer had been yes, counsel puts the question; is it feasible that the impact on the road would have killed people inside the building, when the witness has said that his investigation did not show such a thing. So I object to the question being put, because there's not an adequate predicate for it in the witness's first answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic. Perhaps you should reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, maybe I will reformulate the question on the possibility that this witness would be able to actually investigate anything, because I based myself on what -- on his own experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, reformulate the question then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, according to your experience, you carried out investigations on impact sites. How -- according to your experience, how can fragments or shrapnel coming from a projectile kill anyone who was located behind some kind of barrier, for example, behind a wall?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I would not speculate on -- on that. Because on this scene, we were investigating the impact and what we saw around the impact, and I saw one girl being taken away. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Surely, Mr. Brennskag, maybe I should put my question through counsel. If you could please put the question do him that if he were to determine the direction of the origin of the fire, he would have had to examine also the marks left on the wall, of the shrapnels. I think the witness has already said that he did not do that, so that's one point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Harhoff. That was exactly my line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you heard the question from Judge Harhoff. During your investigation to determine where the shot came from, did you also take the impacts that might have existed on the walls located around the place where the projectile landed?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I understand the question. As far as I know, of course, when you are investigating an impact, you have to look for shrapnels in the nearby areas so you are very sure of -- from where the direction -- the direction the impact is coming. I can't remember what -- if we did that on the walls at this incident. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, one hour and 20 minutes had been allocate the for you. You have about another five minutes left of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I -- by your leave, if I could please have little more time to finish off. I don't really have many topics to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You haven't waited for me to grant the request or to decide whether to grant it. We will grant it, but on no account are we going to have this witness carried over.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, regarding this very specific incident, we, in this courtroom, have really looked into this incident, and this is what I'm interested in: If victims were behind a wall, would the fragment have to go through that wall, penetrate the wall and go through the wall in order to injure the people who were located on the other side of the wall?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: This will only be speculation. Yes, of course, it could be a mirror, a thin wall, depends. This is only speculations, and I don't like to make speculations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: From what I understand, the fragment will have to penetrate the wall, in the first place, to hit someone that would be located behind the wall?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I don't want to answer because this is speculations. I don't know anything about it, at that specific location.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what exactly did you do on the site?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Briefly, we made a crater analysis; and through these analysis, we could find from where the region from where the bomb was launched, just the direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did you draw these conclusions on that very day?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We draw the conclusion of the direction on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do this jointly with the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No. We made our own investigation without inference with the Sarajevan police. Afterwards, we were talking together, of course, and they had the same conclusion. So we were not interfered with when we were doing our job.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the little girl, did you know whether she had been killed or injured only?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: For my own knowledge, she could -- because I didn't see the injuries under the blanket, from my own knowledge, she could only have been - well, only - had been injured. But afterwards through -- I know that she was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On the site, did anyone tell you where that little girl was when the incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yeah. Her father, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: He told us that her girl -- his girl was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you where she was when she was killed?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I can't remember now exactly, but I -- so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But maybe someone else might have told you afterwards?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I -- I said that her father, of course, was talking and said that his girl were killed, but I didn't see it myself that she was dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you remember that you were told she was in her bed.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, one last topic. When you took over your position, when you started working in Bosnia, you were first in Pale. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In the two statements that you gave you're also talking about this. And regarding Pale, you -- your impressions were not very good, rather bad.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Hmm. I have no bad, especially bad memories from my time in Pale. So I don't know what you are up to -- asking me for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on and conclude now, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: First, in your statement of 1996 on page 2, on paragraph 3, you're talking about your experience in Pale. But at the end of the -- middle of the page when talking about the heavy weapons collection points, do you know -- did you find that? It's on the statement of 1996, second page, and it's the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You're talking on that second page about the heavy weapons collection points --

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: -- located on the Serbian side. And are you saying: "[In English] From collection points, weapons were not removed."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. It is so that when we were supposed to inspect the weapon collection points, we have to make an announcement in good advance; and the times when we were able to inspect the weapon collection points, the weapons and the vehicles that should be there were there then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you were not really free to move around. You had restrictions imposed on you, like what happened on the BiH side?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: Yes. We had a lot of restrictions, so we -- and especially we had to make announcement in good time advance before we had to move or make our inspections.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You're also talking about the helicopter that was supposed to evacuate the seriously wounded people towards -- to Serbia or to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG.
utterances.text: This is one of the tragic memories. At that time, it was no-fly zone, but there was agreement that the Bosnian Serbs could take their seriously sick people who needed treatment to Belgrade. I think it was Belgrade. And in my location, we had a small hospital in Pale; and then it was a bigger hospital - I think it was originally for mentally sick people - in Sokolovic, and on announcement to the UN, the Bosnian Serbs had a helicopter taking the patients from Pale. They were landing sometimes at Sokolovic and taking patients to Belgrade. I think it was Belgrade. And our mission was to -- to check that this transport was in order to the agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Isailovic, you have to end now. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: None. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. We will adjourn now and you may leave with us. We'll resume on Monday at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
